client: I just got my final project grade back and it was way lower than I expected. Now I can't stop thinking that maybe I'm just not cut out for this program - like if I can't even do well on this project, how will I handle harder classes? I know therapy is supposed to help with stuff like this, but I'm not sure talking about it will actually change how incompetent I feel.
therapist: It sounds like this grade has really shaken your confidence, and I hear the frustration in your voice as you question your abilities. Let’s explore what evidence you have that you *are* capable—this one project doesn’t define your entire potential. Would it help to break down what specifically felt challenging about it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I know logically that one bad grade doesn't mean I'm a failure, but it's hard not to feel that way when I worked so hard on this project. The worst part is that I actually thought I understood the material, so getting such a low score makes me question if I can trust my own judgment anymore. 

Breaking it down sounds helpful in theory, but I'm worried we'll just end up confirming that I'm not as smart as I thought I was.
therapist: I hear the disappointment in your voice, and it’s understandable to feel this way when something you worked so hard on didn’t turn out as expected. Let’s focus on what you *did* learn from this experience—sometimes setbacks can reveal areas for growth, not just limitations. Would you be open to exploring what might have contributed to the outcome, without letting it define your self-worth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about learning from setbacks, but it's hard not to take this personally. I put everything into this project at work, and now I just feel like maybe I'm not cut out for these kinds of responsibilities. Everyone else seems to handle pressure so much better than I do.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and upset, which tells me how deeply this is affecting you—it’s clear this project meant a lot. Comparing yourself to others often leaves us feeling worse; let’s focus instead on what *you* need to feel more confident in these situations. What would support look like for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you noticing how upset I am about this project. It's just...I worked so hard on it, and seeing others do better with what seems like less effort really stings. I don't even know what support would look like - part of me thinks I should just be able to handle this better on my own.
therapist: I hear both the hurt and frustration in your voice—it’s especially painful when effort doesn’t seem to match outcomes. That desire to "handle it on your own" is understandable, but even the strongest people benefit from support. Would it help to explore what "handling it better" realistically looks like, rather than holding yourself to an impossible standard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I’ve always felt like I *should* be able to handle things on my own, like needing help is a sign of weakness. But I’m tired of feeling stuck and like I’m failing at everything. The idea of “handling it better” sounds good, but I’m not even sure what that would look like—it feels like another thing I’ll just fall short of.
therapist: Your voice sounds strained and quick—I can hear how exhausted you are from carrying this weight alone. That belief about needing to be self-sufficient is so common, yet it often leaves us feeling more isolated in our struggles. Let’s gently challenge that idea: what if asking for help is actually a strength, a way to grow rather than a sign of falling short?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying about asking for help being a strength, but it just feels so unnatural to me. Every time I think about reaching out, this voice in my head says I should be able to handle things on my own. And honestly, when I've tried asking for help before, people either didn't understand or made me feel like a burden.
therapist: Your voice sounds hesitant and quiet—I can hear how vulnerable this makes you feel, especially when past experiences with reaching out haven’t gone well. That critical inner voice can be so convincing, but let’s examine the evidence: have there been *any* times when asking for help didn’t leave you feeling like a burden? Even small examples might help us challenge that belief.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess there was one time when I asked my sister for help moving last year. She actually seemed happy to do it, but I still felt guilty afterward. Like I owed her something, even though she said it was no big deal. It's hard to trust that people genuinely want to help without expecting something in return.
therapist: It sounds like even when help was offered freely, like with your sister, that lingering guilt made it hard to fully accept it. Your voice brightened a bit as you recalled her willingness, though—what might it mean that she genuinely seemed happy to assist? Perhaps this could be a starting point for exploring how to trust that support can be given without strings attached.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know my sister genuinely wanted to help, but it’s hard to shake the feeling that I’m burdening her, even if she says she’s happy to assist. I keep thinking, "What if she’s just being nice?" or "What if she resents me later?" I want to trust that support can be given freely, but it feels like I’m always waiting for the other shoe to drop.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and rushed—I can hear how much this doubt weighs on you, even when kindness is offered freely. That fear of "the other shoe dropping" is so relatable, yet it keeps you from fully receiving support that could lighten your load. Let’s explore this: if your sister *genuinely* wanted to help, what would it take for you to believe her—not just in that moment, but afterward too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It’s hard for me to trust that she genuinely wants to help. Even when she says it, I keep thinking she’s just being nice or feels obligated, and she’ll regret it later. I don’t know how to let myself believe her—it feels like I’m waiting for her to prove me right by pulling away eventually.
therapist: Your voice sounds strained and quick—I can hear how much this fear of being let down is gripping you, making it hard to accept kindness at face value. That anticipation of rejection must be exhausting to carry. Let’s pause here: what would it feel like to sit with the possibility—just the possibility—that your sister’s care might be as genuine as it seems?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know...I guess sitting with that possibility makes me feel kind of naked and exposed. Like if I let myself believe she really cares, then it'll hurt ten times worse when she eventually proves me wrong. It's happened so many times before with other people.  

I want to trust her, but my brain keeps replaying all those past times when people said they cared and then just...disappeared. It's like my body physically braces for the blow even when nothing bad is happening right now.
therapist: I hear how small and vulnerable your voice gets as you describe this—it’s clear those past hurts still feel raw, making it so hard to let your guard down even with your sister. That instinct to brace yourself is protective, but I wonder if we could gently explore how this pattern might be keeping you from the very connection you long for. Would it feel safe to name what you *do* trust about your relationship with her, even if it’s just one small thing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
